8.t: Lula White's house: how the girls dressed and the parlor
8.s: Garland describes the girls' short childlike dresses, lace stockings and bows at Lula White's place, the mirrors, coloured lights and the price of beer.
8.q: Looked like a little baby, you know? You ever see a little baby when they put some clothes on a baby? Kidding how they kind of stuck up? Oh, like that, you know. All silk, you know. And these stockings, like I'm telling you. That time used to have what they called lace stockings. You know, open-led…

8.t: More on the girls' costumes and the women at Lula White's
8.s: The interviewer presses for detail on the dresses, stockings and underwear; women of all colours, all pretty.
8.q: No, not those people. I wasn't no real stylish. Because when they come in there, they come in there with that little short dress, you understand? Yeah.

8.t: Customers and George Lambert's gambling house
8.s: Customers were white men; Garland only delivered clothes for gambler George Lambert; other houses lined the street.
8.q: You know, no, no, man. You tried? No. Oh, try what? I'd better not try to go in there. It looked like I want to go there for anything. No? I started bringing a message. Then they come talking about the oil. They said, go with her. Shit. I used to bring George Lambert. I used to bring the clothes…

8.t: Tom Anderson's places and their string bands
8.s: Description of Tom Anderson's saloons on Basin Street and Rampart, and the string bands there.
8.q: wrestling yeah yeah she had one at Bishon in uh Everville it run from Everville to Basin Street on Everville uh-huh uh-huh Franklin to Basin uh-huh then the other one was Ramport Canal or right off of Canal

8.t: Addresses, the Guidry and Allen nightclub before Chicago
8.s: Where Garland lived on Cleveland Avenue and Villa Street, and the upstairs club at Guidry and Allen where he played before leaving for Chicago.
8.ch: New Orleans bands, brass bands and learning bass
8.q: Well, what you call them, is that? There's a ballroom on the corner, and upstairs used to be a little club, nightclub. I was playing up there when I left to go to Chicago. Guidry and Allen. Oh. Guidry and Allen.

248.t: King's ballroom, Oaky Pope and women hustling between districts
248.s: Dawson recalls the Italian ballroom owner King's place and its bartender Oaky Pope, and how groups of women moved from downtown to uptown hustling.
248.ch: The district underworld and street musicians
248.q: That's right. Then they'd go from one place to the other. What did they walk around the way? You see, like, they'd be around 25. Yeah. They'd decide to go over, over cross Canal Street and go by, uh, uh, what you call, uh, uh, the Italian fella had that ballroom at the corner of, um, Gasket and,…

248.t: Pete Lala, the 25s and its gambling room
248.s: Questions about McNicious, Lala's and the 25s: gambling, the bartender Henry Bowser, whether Oliver played there.
248.q: The only ones I know, and I practically know that place, from around there, from Iverville, the Rays all the way up to Ramport Street. Iverville, Bienville, I don't know no McNicious place, the only thing. Lala, I know Pete Lala, there was, like I told you, Lala was on the Rays in Iverville.

248.t: Tom Anderson's two places and the band's role
248.s: Anderson's places on Basin Street and Rampart; his influence, birthday parties and money, and the singing waiters.
248.q: Yeah, yeah. Then they... Well, frankly, old Tom Anderson can do anything he want in the city because he was a big... He was a big boss. Yeah, he was a big boss in the city, yeah. Anything he... When they would go around raiding any place, they never bought his place. No one did, not Tom Anderson.…

248.t: The Jip the Blood killing and the district closings
248.s: They discuss the killing, and how the district was repeatedly closed and reopened; Dawson was not there.
248.q: Oh, yes. That's, that's, that's, that's, uh, I didn't know much about him, but I, I remember the time, you know, when he, when he did do all that killing.

293.t: Cooney, Lulu White and an actress in France
293.s: He cannot place Cooney, then recounts an actress in France asking about Lulu White of 235 Basin Street and his visits in the kitchen.
293.ch: Pianists, the district and Stormy Weather
293.q: Yeah, the actress. She said, I've been there and stopped there. I said, well, I know her. She said, you speak French mighty good. I told her I speak French too. I mean, they always.

293.t: Fourth reel: the Alley cabaret and Andre Dominguez
293.s: New reel begins; questions about the Alley cabaret where his brother dealt four-card money, and Andre Dominguez.
293.q: Uh, yeah. Do I really? Did you know a cabaret called the alley? The alley? The alley. Cabaret? Just a drinking place. I don't know. There are so many places.

293.t: Uncle in the district and Lulu White's wig
293.s: His uncle lived in the district; he recalls Fess Minetta, pay of a dollar a night and Lulu White, arguing about her skin colour and her blonde wig.
293.q: Oh yeah, I met Fess a long time. I mean, Minetta, I met him oh years ago. And in them days they were getting but a dollar a night.

293.t: Ida Jackson's house and his band
293.s: Played many jobs at Ida Jackson's house with pianist Herbert Bloom, Albert Burbank and others, and heard Willie Jackson at Tom Anderson's.
293.q: Yeah, she had a house and we used to play there. And our piano player was, his name was Herbert Bloom. He's in California right now. Good piano player.

21.t: Layout of 25s on Franklin Street: bar, booth and gambling room
21.s: Manetta sketches the Franklin Street 25 club, with its bar, glass booth with a piano and the gambling room where Joe Oliver and Jelly Roll played pool and cards.
21.ch: Dreamland and the Tuxedo dance hall
21.q: Not yet. Now watch. I'll describe it. Here's Franklin Street. Mm-hmm. Here's the door. Right. As you go in the door, there's the bar. There, right to your left, that's where the booth is built. Oh, I see. Right from the door. Mm-hmm. Nice glass. You know it had glasses in it? Oh, I see. It's just a…

21.t: Playing piano at Gertrude Dix's next to Anderson's Annex
21.s: He played piano for Gertrude Dix's house beside Tom Anderson's Annex Saloon, then was sent to Anderson's son-in-law's cabaret.
21.ch: Annex, Cadillac and the Ory-Oliver band
21.q: Mr. Tom Anderson sent for me. His... My wife's... ...lady friend, I'll say. ...was Gertrude Dix. She ran... The house was called a brass railing. It was right next... ...to Mr. Anderson's Annex Saloon. Mr. Anderson's Annex Saloon. And, uh... I went to wake over there for her. Miss Dix. Well, I…

21.s: The Annex had floor-level playing, a bar, a cabaret room with floor show, and a kitchen.
21.ch: Annex, Cadillac and the Ory-Oliver band
21.q: What's the cabaret? First, the saloon. Oh, the cabaret. Well, the cabaret was, and so you enter the saloon, and right inside of the saloon was the cabaret, where they entertained that, singing and dance. Like a floor show, you know? Yeah. That was another room.

635.t: Tonks and barrelhouses: drinks and the back dance room
635.s: Prices of whiskey, beer and Angelica wine, what barrelhouses and tonks looked like, and the piano in the back room.
635.ch: Cabarets and the Red Light District
635.q: Yeah. Well it's not a, you couldn't say it's a 12 bar blues because they'll all make 20 bars and they'll say this. I see. And it's just very slow, you walk into that same temple all night long. And the places they call tunks. Now a tunk, you'll know you won't know what a tunk is. A tunk is where…

635.t: Girls' dress, the cribs and the Hans Nagel cabaret
635.s: Describes the dancers' dress, the cribs in the red light district, and names the cabaret as Huntz and Nagel's, with its owners.
635.ch: Cabarets and the Red Light District
635.q: What do they wear? They wear like nice gay them dresses, clean. It's regular dresses. Yeah. See women's land made their money on their legs, big legs. And you see the legs up to the air back in those days, man. Rain, I used to pay a dime to go downtown, a nickel. I used to see women get on the…

635.t: Inside the Customs and Liberty cabaret and selling drinks
635.s: Description of the cabaret, police detail, bandstand, tables, how short numbers made customers buy beer, and champagne prices.
635.ch: Cabarets and the Red Light District
635.q: Well the cabaret, the cabaret then was about... It was just a little bit wider and the hangover club. Uh huh. See? And just about that long.

56.s: The district places were open day and night, with no doors on the bars.
56.q: You know, I could get a job. Wasn't there any doors in the place. The place, the place was open 24 hours a day. No doors on the bar. Is that so? No. In the district, you mean? Mm-hmm.

56.t: How the girls dressed at Lulu White's
56.s: Ory describes the women in robes and house clothes.
56.ch: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
56.q: Or the negligee and the robe and things, you know. Mm-hmm. They get house clothes, you know. I mean... But they weren't all dressed up. Oh, no, not in... No? No, not in evening gowns or things like that. No, no, yeah. They were upstairs. When the guys walk in, they come in down like race horses.…

56.s: Ory describes the corner building, bar and raised bandstand.
56.q: No, I think Tin Angel, a little larger. A little larger. Was it shaped the same way? Yeah, square. Square. And the bar was in the front, you know.

198.t: How many bands worked the District
198.s: Barnes says about two dozen bands played in the Red District, in houses and honky-tonks.
198.q: Yeah, good many musicians. Most every house had it. Had music up there. Every house, you know every place. Gammon houses.

198.s: Allen asks how many musicians worked; Barnes says mostly cabarets and tunks, explains the difference and names the spots.
198.q: Well, the brass band wasn't a brass band was equalized to the string band. That band was splitting. See, if a man played a funeral or prayed or something like that, well, that day, he'd come to that job that night. See, so you couldn't count that. There's two.

198.t: The band at the Golden Room with cousin Mitchell Frazier
198.s: Barnes names his cousin Frazier and the Golden Room band; the talk turns to the quiet neighborhood around it.
198.ch: Blues, cabarets and the Golden Room
198.q: Well I think so, pretty much. We used to fight the blues, but from what I could understand, we were the best blues player. I had me, and my cousin Mitchell Frazier. I had a mic on drums, he's dead. Wouldn't you on climbing? Oh no. Something. I was on climbing.

769.t: Back doors, Lula White's and Emma Johnson's shows
769.s: He only went in through the back of houses like Lula White's and Emma Johnson's, and recalls Emma Johnson's notorious stunts.
769.q: I never did see what the front part looked like. I've always heard what it looked like but I never got in the front. And I used to go by old Emma Johnson. She had the old play step right next to the fire engine house that used to be out there. I was on Basin and Corn Eye. Well, I used to say the…

769.t: Geography of the district and the bell system
769.s: He maps the area he was allowed to go in, describes cribs and apartment houses, and explains the bell-ring system for picking up orders.
769.q: No. I never got that far. The farthest I went was to Franklin, back to Robinson. Yeah. And from, I'd say from St. Louis to Iberville. That was the first, that was our locale, you know, because they didn't allow you to go around in front of them houses.

249.t: Tom Anderson's place, its management and bootleg liquor
249.s: Tom Anderson was boss of the district; the band was paid with no instruction; liquor was served in milk bottles; singer Willie Jackson.
249.q: Well years I have to give up, he had his son lost to run a father named George Delsick. Oh yeah, I heard it. Used to run it, yeah. Used to run it. I worked there a long time for him. He was a nice friend. You never know, he'd never tell the band nothing. Never tell the band nothing. They'd give you…

249.t: When he started at Anderson's and the district closing
249.s: He started late 1918; the district partly closed around 1915-16 and reopened after the war.
249.q: Yeah. And bootleggers time, I was around 19. Yeah. You still had a chance. You still got them now, for that concern. Yeah, I guess.

474.s: Rampart Street's commercial district, with the Pelican, Savoy and Roof Garden.
474.ch: Hometown ties, community and favorite players
474.q: Yeah, the Pelican was right there. Yeah. Their story was right there. They had a band. The Roof Garden had a band around the corner. Right around the corner. They had the Savoy. You ever heard of that? No. You know where the Omen Hall at? No. The Omen Hall is still there. What's it called now? The…

474.t: The Tuxedo, Gene Hall and Kaiser Joseph
474.s: The Tuxedo behind the station on Canal, Gene Hall, and Kaiser Joseph's late-1920s work.
474.ch: Kid Rena, the Cadillac and Jones's sons
474.q: Gene Hall, I know Gene Hall. Yeah, piano. Yeah, and somebody else, I forgot that was a tuxedo. Where was that? That was around in there behind, the southern station on Canal Street at that time. Used to have a station on Canal Street.

430.t: Layout of Tom Anderson's place on Rampart
430.s: The interviewers ask about the inside of Anderson's and compare it with the 25.
430.q: no not that I do offer no did you play in the annex at all oh in anderson all that's all to know i don't know but i mean how about in anderson's okay that answer yeah ramparts you don't want to ramp up yeah that place here not at the annex we're gonna work at the annex i never did

430.t: Anderson's bar, bandstand, floor and kitchen
430.s: Details of the bar on the left, sawdust and spittoons, the bandstand facing the door and the hall and kitchen behind.
430.q: Was the book when you come in the door was the bar on the right or on the left? On the left side on the left side. That's right. That's right. The bar was on the other side. That's right.

765.t: Ice cream customers, prices and the plush houses
765.s: Selling to prostitutes, prices, houses on Basin and Franklin Streets.
765.q: You know some of them with... They had to put some on a book and I just... I gave it to them. I didn't charge them. And then they finally... Finally they caught a trick or two and they sort of paid me off.

765.t: Old Legends, Sweet Potato Inn, Vanity and Silver Slipper
765.s: Homebrew joints and dance halls with Lillard Prima, Al Durier and others.
765.ch: New Orleans scene and jazz club
765.q: No, the majority of them are in the 40s, 50s, 60s, on up. Did you ever go to the old legends that Almanaster and Murray? No, just one time, because at the time I was over at the Legion, I couldn't get down there where I wanted to. I used to hear a lot about it. I mean, after the dance hall was shut…

629.t: Playing for Lula White and Tony Jackson in the mansions
629.s: Picou played clarinet and piano in the front parlor at Lula White's; talk of Tony Jackson's tunes, Jelly Roll Morton, hours and no shows.
629.q: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Well, did you ever play in any of those mansion houses in the district there, Alphonse? I played for Lula White. She had a band in there too, didn't you? Lula White. Lula White. Uh-huh. Lula White. I thought about pretty woman, can you show? Lula White. Yeah, look…

629.t: The bar building, its bandstand and the piano
629.s: Talk about how the back of the daughter's bar was once outdoors, the owner, big Joe moving the piano, the bandstand and its cabinets.
629.q: Where the bar is was outdoors, you told us once. Didn't you? Where the bar is was really outdoors in the back? Yeah. They added that. Yeah, that was outdoors there. Yeah. Then they added that part. Yeah. Yeah, that was outdoors there. Yeah. Then they added that part. Well, there's a little bit of a…

279.s: Hug recalls walking Basin Street as a boy when Storyville was officially closed but still active.
279.q: Well, I could say this, that I can remember walking around in that area, but of course you must remember that it closed 1918. That's correct. According to what we know or what we read about.

279.t: The original 25 Club and the Honeysuckle Inn
279.s: Two rival roadhouses in Prohibition days, where everything cost 25 cents.
279.ch: Dance halls and clubs of the 1930s
279.q: Yeah, that's right. We had a good little band at the original 25 Club. That was back off the Pontchartrain Road where the Honeysuckle Inn was. You may have heard of the Honeysuckle Inn. The Honeysuckle Inn and the original 25 Club were right across from each other. Is that? Sharky opened at the…

632.t: More journal entries and visits to a house
632.s: Journal items on the funeral, Roger Wolfe interview, a Storyville house on Esplanade and a place they visited.
632.q: photographed that I don't know uh has anybody I'm sure we've talked about this before although not on tape has anybody ever uh explored the possibility of looking in of the look files

632.t: Tape check and the decor of old clubs
632.s: After a recorder check, Steinau recalls the old-fashioned decor of the clubs and neighbours' remarks about parties.
632.q: Oh, okay. I don't think I said this on the earlier tape, but I remember enjoying what I felt was an atmosphere and a decor in a lot of these places that went back for a long time. Mm-hmm. There were cut out... Mm-hmm. There were jigsaw wooden decorations in some of the places. Oh, yeah. There was a…

84.t: Tom Anderson's place and old Rampart Street
84.s: He describes Anderson's as the most exclusive spot, other nearby places, and the empty lots on Rampart.
84.ch: Armstrong, the Elite and New Orleans scene
84.q: Well, that was about the most exclusive place they had around here at that time. Uh, Tom Anderson. Uh, Tom Anderson. Uh, it stayed back because, uh, we had another place there on, uh, Bienville between Ramport and Burgundy. Oh, I forgot, I forgot the name of the place. But anyway, that was where…

84.t: The Hummingbird and the wide-open district
84.s: He describes the Hummingbird nightclub on Bienville and the lively district crowd, girls and pimps spending money.
84.q: There was a lot of dancing and drinking. The thing about it was when them girls come out of them cribs. They go home and take their bath and straighten their self up and put on them clothes. And come out there and just throw away some money.

894.t: W. C. Handy and the roadhouse called Pee Wee on Beale Street
894.s: Lewis knew Handy, who started at Pee Wee, a wide-open roadhouse on Beale Street where musicians hung out.
894.q: Oh, I know him, sure. Mm-hmm. He started here on Beale Street, a place called Pee Wee up there on Beale Street through there. Of course, the fact about it, that's all our hang-up was right there. That's where all of us started at, right there.

894.t: The Monarch joint, Winding Boy, and tape ending
894.s: Lewis describes the Monarch as a big rough joint with gambling; he does not know Winding Boy, and the tape runs out.
894.q: that was a large joint that was one of them of the deep joints the monarch he used to they had with that

650.t: Eloise Blackenstein's sporting house and the beautiful Louise Aberdey
650.s: He describes a prominent Black madam's house at Gasquet and Villere and a beautiful woman there who affected him personally.
650.q: No heard of Eloise Blackenstein. That was a big time woman, Eloise Blackenstein. She was a big time. Sporting house she had. Blackenstein? Eloise Blackenstein. Big time. Big time. Big time. Big time as she was.

650.t: Sam Henry and the public houses of the district
650.s: Amacker describes Sam Henry as an old Ravage Street player and the sporting houses lining the streets, with prices and some of the sex shows he took part in.
650.q: He's from here, right from here. Sam Henry, he's from here. Old time player, old Ravage Street player, years ago. In those days, a neighborhood like this, like you see this neighborhood. Both sides of these streets here, both sides of these streets here would be what you call public houses. See, in…

247.t: Tom Anderson's cabarets and Paul Dominguez
247.s: Asked about Storyville cabarets, he says he played for Tom Anderson and for Paul Dominguez, who had cabarets on Rampart-area streets, and describes the bandstands and the crowds.
247.q: He means in the district. Oh! I played with Anderson. I played with him. I played with him on the right part between Canal and Abraville. On that side of the back. Anderson. I played with him. I mean this fellow, Paul Dominguez. I know him at Dwyer. You know him? He heard all of him. He did Paul…

178.t: Herbert Smith and the Last Roundup
178.s: They recall saxophonist Herbert Smith, his restaurant and bartending job, and the Last Roundup place.
178.q: It was on Benville and near Dauphin. Yeah. He had Smith's restaurant right here on Johnson and Laparuse. Oh he was a fine-signist.

181.t: Downtown Canal Street memories and Tom Anderson's
181.s: Mac remembers Canal Street shops, shining shoes, Tom Anderson's and the waiter Boleg.
181.q: Oh, I remember pretty good. I shined shoes, I was all in the house. So you take where Cotton's jewelry store, that used to be a barber shop on that corner. Right on the canal. And you take where the Lois State, that used to be a shooting gallery. And where the Sanger is now, that was something like…

917.t: Franklin Street musicians and Tick Chambers; band photo question
917.s: Keppard names players on Franklin Street around Tick Chambers and the district closing; the tape ends with a question about a band photo with Roy Palmer.
917.q: Oakland right where Crozac is. Dates have their back entrance that Hall is given back there. Old man Umpra used to play with dear with Tick Chambers. You heard to talk about Tick Chambers? Yes, the Oakland Well, Tickshaber was playing cornet, and this fellow, Lawrence Dewitt, was playing clarinet…

761.t: Big 25: bands, gambling and the private piano room
761.s: Bocage and Alfred Williams played the Big 25 back room; the wine room piano was used for private guests.
761.q: No, they had music. They mostly had three, four pieces there. It was three good man's that they had. They had 피shaw and Alfred Williams and Charlie Bocage on banjo. It was three good pieces they had.

891.t: Louis Dumaine's band at the Royal Garden
891.s: Dumaine had a nice swinging band at the Royal Garden, though not a rough 'bohemian' one.
891.q: Louis Dumaine swung as this, swung as this. He used to play at the Royal Garden. Remember I was a kid and the Royal Garden was on Drive, between Drive and Rampart. And he had a nice band. Nice band, I mean. Wasn't no Bauhaus, you know. No, he wasn't no Bauhaus. He played nice music, wasn't no…

752.t: Playing the Storyville district and chalking the tricks
752.s: Pops describes the district's pleasures, and how he and Louis Nelson chalked tricks on the wall while playing; a visitor, Bob Campbell, drops in.
752.q: Yeah so, yeah there was some, there was some beautiful days back in them days. Beautiful women, man. Oh. Yeah? And then there's Ray La Dixie. You had anything you want. And for years no band, you couldn't get a band out of New Orleans because it was too great.

624.t: Abbie at the Hotsi Totsi, pedal-note trombone and prohibition clubs
624.s: Brunies recalls Abbie's horn tricks at a speakeasy, his own trick of playing trombone on cornet with pedal notes, and clubs along Dauphine Street in prohibition.
624.ch: Playing in clubs and Mardi Gras
624.q: I don't know if Abby ever told you about... How you used to jam the silk paintings up in there. No, I don't believe so. They had a place on Common Street, right off the dryings. In the speaking easy days. Called a Hotsi Totsi. And the racehorse men used to go up in there. And Abby, Jan, that silk…

1000.t: Pajeaud's rank and the Liberty and Iberville saloon run by Frank Early
1000.s: Pajeaud is remembered as a good player; they try to place the Pete Lala-area saloon, now a parking lot or grocery, run by a policeman.
1000.q: Oh yeah, he was, he had a, say, a cranny like a pipe. Yeah, he still has a little. He had that cranny like a pipe. Yeah, he used to play that drum. Yeah, he used to play. He could play too. Yeah. And him and Louis was good friends. They used to play each other, help each other out around, around…

568.s: Russell and Hightower work out the location of the all-white cabaret near Canal Street and Customhouse, and confirm the name Grunewald's Casino.
568.q: Yeah, it was a cabaret. But we, at those times they used flow shows and choruses. Yeah, what corner was that on? That was on the downtown, back of town by the corner. Downtown. Downtown side.

969.t: Drinking at dances and cabarets during Prohibition
969.s: No bars at private dances; bring your own bottle; cabarets like Tranchina's and the Halfway House; the Little Club as the priciest.
969.q: Well, there were no bars in the dancers that I'm talking about. Remember, these were dancers that were given by, in most cases, private clubs and no bars. The bottle was out in the automobile and he went out during intermission and got a couple of slugs and... But, uh... They were never given...…

762.t: The Alley cabaret behind Seminard Market
762.s: Purnell clarifies the Alley was at St. Bernard and Claiborne behind the market, not in Storyville, where he heard Guy Kelly.
762.q: No, no. The alley was on St. Bernard and Claiborne. Right behind, that's where the Seminard Market was. And in the back of the Seminard Market they had allies leading from Seminard off to Claiborne. And right in the back there they had a cabaret.

1.t: Cook and Copperwire, notorious women of the district
1.s: Friedlander describes two rough women of the red-light district who were buddies; one is now blind and sick, and he talks about her time in Charity Hospital.
1.q: She's an old lady and you have to be cooking. And you have to be cooking. And you have to be cooking.

251.t: The de Mausoliere family and Claiborne Avenue saloons
251.s: They discuss the family that ran joints along Claiborne, a mortuary site, and the women in one family. Albert recalls saloon keeper Zemo and fetching his father.
251.q: With Laud. That's right. That's his mother's place. We talk about Asano. She was married to Asano and then she married Emil Laud. And now she's married to George Lopez. The first two months was the past.

401.t: The Court Tavern with Tony and Jimmy Cooper
401.s: Williams and Tony worked in a gay-nineties tavern built for them behind the Court of Two Sisters on Bourbon Street.
401.q: Huh? That room we were in. Jimmy Cooper built that little place in the back. You're talking about the place on Bourbon? Yeah.

268.t: Origin of the name La Vida, the owner, and substituting at the Budweiser
268.s: They discuss the name and owner of La Vida, how Handy hired him, and his Saturday work at the Budweiser.
268.ch: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
268.q: That was after, you know, I left and started working for the Power of Life Company. Then I used to go there and rest on Saturday nights like that, Sunday.

276.t: Few Clothes Willie and finding the cafes across from the Big 25
276.s: Trying to place Few Clothes' cafe, Mouton's Cafe, the Hummingbird and Entertainers Cabarets near Iberville and Franklin, torn down for a project.
276.q: I know one guy used to be around there, they called him Few Clothes Willie I remember that too He used to call him Few Clothes Willie I don't know what happened

23.t: Prostitution in Armstrong's neighborhood before and after Storyville
23.s: After Storyville was legalized, the uptown black prostitutes moved to cribs there, so arrests fell.
23.q: And they had apartments, you know, and places where they lived. However, when Storyville was, was legalized, see, then the police came down on all those women and tried to stop that.

432.t: The Dog House and Tuxedo dance hall with Octave Crosby
432.s: He describes working the Dog House and Tuxedo for Eddie Groeschel, and the earlier Entertainers lineup with David Jones.
432.q: No, I played for Dog House and I played, when that closed down I went down the next block with Octave Crosby, Joe Harris. You remember Octave Crosby that died? Yeah. Yeah, down the next block. We were working for Elie Groeschel, you know where the Dog House we started working for. Who's the Dog…

713.t: Rudy Doody's and the gypsy tea room
713.s: Nelson and Collins place Rudy Doody's at Sanana and Robinson and distinguish it from the gypsy tea room, where rooming houses now stand.
713.q: no that's the Rudy Doody that's on this street the gypsy tea room was on it's on Zirano and Sanana Villarreal Center

876.t: St. Louis: Tom Turpin, Jazzland and the district
876.s: The interviewer asks about Turpin's Jazzland, the Booker T. Washington Theater and the St. Louis red-light district; St. Cyr recalls the layout but never heard Turpin play.
876.q: No, no. They put the damp on Prohibition End. I mean, the damp went on while we went to St. Louis. And I used to go to the chauffeur's club very often.

819.t: Tom Anderson, Basin Street cabarets and policemen in cabarets
819.s: Tom Anderson's cabaret, Josie Arlington, and the policeman kept in every cabaret.
819.q: he was a big man who was a politician and he had everything to say I knew him I only saw him yeah because I worked as I say only one door away from him and I worked in the black cat for about a

283.t: The Tin Roof and its sprinkler rain trick
283.s: He explains the Tin Roof on Baronne Street owned by Tony DeNapoli, where sprinklers on the roof made fake rain to keep the crowd.
283.ch: Reel two to four: pay, tailgate and style
283.q: They didn't know that, huh? Nobody. And right now, I bet a lot of people can't tell you what I'm telling you. I told people that and they said they can't believe it.

10.s: A brief fragment about a barroom on Custom House Street.
10.q: Yes, that was a barroom on Iberville Street, or Custom House Street, I should say, and I think at the Corner of Liberty there was a barroom.

49.s: Hazel says places with music stayed open until about 1929 and mentions Tom Anderson, Willie Piazza and the Entertainers.
49.q: It was. But it, it, it, it, what happened after that? It was, it was open back there for years after that, but it wasn't as open, you know, as it, as it was written in. It, it, it, it, other words it was, it was on a, it had a few places back there. They had a place called The Entertainers. And…

878.s: They place the Ringside, later Pete Herman's, earlier the Orchard.
878.ch: Sharky Bonanno, Sidney Arodin and the Ringside
878.q: I remember when it was the orchard.

820.t: 25 Cent Club and the Honeysuckle Inn rivalry
820.s: Frank worked at the 25 Cent Club across from the Honeysuckle Inn; stories of flagging cars with lanterns and hot bowls of ice during Prohibition.
820.q: They used to put the ice in hot bowls and put the bowls in the oven and the ice was two bits of bowl. Two bits of bowl. So they'd melt. There was no liquor in those days. That was prohibition. And the only thing they could get was two bits for the bowl of ice. So they'd get that hot bowl out there.

572.t: Eating at Thompson's, Child's and Exchange Alley
572.s: Musicians met for breakfast at Thompson's, and he recalls oyster sandwiches during Prohibition.
572.ch: Wider talk: bands, places and players
572.q: What was that, about 20 years ago? Everybody used to tell, well, sometimes, uh, sometimes we'd go to Child's restaurant that was, uh, uh, across from Royal Island there, or at least, uh, what, what, what street, Champ Street, right up, around Camp and, and Canal Street there, that's where Child's…

176.t: About two years at the Rialto and the history of Luchenbach's
176.s: Billie stayed two years at the Rialto, then describes Luchenbach's old folks home restaurant and dance hall.
176.q: He must've worked with some good bands. Ah, man. Well, I don't think he worked with too many bands. Well, of course, what I mean, because I know that when he worked with Santa, they stayed on that boat that's so long, you know. I don't think that he worked around with too many bands. So, after they…

128.s: Percy and Jim describe the honky tonks as cabarets with dancing and girls.
128.ch: Social life of old New Orleans
128.q: It's a regular cabaret. It's a cabaret. It's a be dance. With the girls, man.

884.t: Algiers and New Orleans as one city; Rampart Street cabarets
884.s: Algiers saw itself as part of one city; he remembers Rampart Street and the blue light district cabarets where string bands worked.
884.ch: Algiers parades and the wider city
884.q: Well, we knew it was all one big city, you know. It's different ones like Jefferson Powers and Algiers, but that was different than that, you know. But like New Orleans, you know, over here, we always think we're the one city. Yeah.

780.t: Where he works now and the Fairmont hotel name
780.s: Chat about his current job at the Fairmont, formerly the Roosevelt, and its owner.
780.ch: Piano, Guitar Slim and personal life
780.q: I think his name is, uh, let's see what's his name. Oh boy. Oh, mm. I can't think of his name. Oh, well. I don't know. Yeah, I think this guy is from Los Angeles. Or San Francisco, I rather. Oh, yeah.

196.t: The Tango Belt and cafes near the district
196.s: Leclerc explains the Tango Belt cafes (Anderson's, the Pup Cafe, the Cadillac) lay across Rampart from the district.
196.q: Well, the Tango Belt was on the other side of the road, on the other side of the district. That's what they called it. In those days, that's what they called it.

298.t: Club Arlington's name, Tom Anderson and Decatur Street
298.s: Talk of Tom Anderson, Josie Arlington and how Decatur Street held all the clubs.
298.q: I've got a picture of him. Because he had that club, he was operating that club, and he had a club on wood. He was operating that club on wood. And Andrew Anderson was working at the club on wood. And Andrew Anderson was working at the club on wood. And we was at the club all on the thing. Yeah,…

909.t: Come Clean hall and the East Green gambling joints
909.s: Morris describes the Come Clean hall, the East Green gambling area and Harvey Canal night house where he played with Wooden Joe.
909.ch: Childhood and early music in Algiers
909.q: No, it's over from the courthouse You know, way over on this side Oh, I know They used to have a green back there And gambling of all kinds Used to be there And people from all over Used to come there and gamble And so That's why I used to play Play there too I used to play music At Harvest Canal…

710.t: Gasquet Street, Franklin Street, the 25s and Rampart Street places
710.s: Bailey describes dancing, gambling and hustling women around Gasquet and Franklin, the gambling 25s, and music at the Pelican and on Rampart.
710.q: Well they had a boardroom with plenty dancing, gambling, dancing. Some of the places they had fish fries around there. People selling their fish. And their little home brew there them days. Way back around 1919. They had all that.

300.t: Red Onion Drag and the old house of detention district
300.s: Humphrey explains the Red Onion Drag name came from a red house behind the house of detention near James Alley, and recalls advertising wagons there.
300.ch: Ann Cook session and Buddy Petit stories
300.q: Yeah, James Alley. And that's in the James Alley. You go across there. Then you get into James Alley. Tough part back there.

708.t: Locating the early Panama and Deluxe on 35th Street
708.s: They sort out whether the old Panama and Deluxe were upstairs or downstairs at 35th and State; her Panama was the later one on 58th.
708.q: It was downstairs, I think. Yeah. I think it was downstairs, but it was right there at 35th and stayed. No, it was upstairs. On the corner.

147.t: Hustlers and number men at the Vendome Hotel
147.s: Crawford describes the numbers bankers who stayed at the hotels and the Core and Claw families of Buffalo, with a detour on food at the Howard.
147.q: Oh, you had guys, hustlers there and everything. Person like like Jones Brothers out of Chicago, big number men. Now, you can erase that. And [Ruby] Harris out of Pittsburgh. When they hit Buffalo -- that's the only place I knew them, and I wanted to know more of them because they were

76.t: Madames' stables of girls and the welcoming committees
76.s: Marge explains that in New Orleans and East St. Louis madams brought their girls to dances to meet musicians, later replaced by the young welcoming committees of Basie's day.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: But the musician was always sharp looking. Yes. And another thing, well women nowadays who do hustle and are prostitutes don't have time to hang around any Roseland and any in front of bandstands.

112.t: Playing piano 'professor' in Atlantic City bawdy houses
112.s: Hired from the corner to play in white and Black brothels, he describes the screens, the acts and the tips in summer and the slump in winter.
112.q: We're up there, see. Now, we used to come down there to play a little piano. So, in Atlantic City, the only way I could make a living, I used to, to eat and sleep, after trying to be a little pimp or something around there. See, was to stand on the corner of North Carolina and Baltic and, up North…
